#5517. On theCUBE Pod: Blue wave sends AI stock plunging

The very blue results of last week’s midterms have sent technology investors into a tailspin.

With many successful candidates running on platforms opposing data centers and calling for greater restrictions on artificial intelligence, investors anticipate a slowdown in AI spending. Tech stocks fell, with a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap, and the Nasdaq dropped more than 5.5%.

“Yesterday was a bloodbath,” said John Furrier (pictured), executive analyst for theCUBE Research. “It was brutal here and the tech stocks got pounded. 41 states had data centers on the ballot. They all lost or won, depending how you look at it. Now it’s so mainstream, it’s a political football. So you’re starting to see the reality of AI. It’s hitting everybody. Everyone is impacted.”

On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (pictured, right), chief analyst for theCUBE Research, discussed the fallout from the midterms and whether or not AI companies will really suffer in the long term. They also explored who will own the “system of intelligence” that will govern enterprise AI.

After the “bloodbath” last week, the question remains: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Despite the shockwaves from the midterms, theCUBE’s researchers are predicting a longer path toward monetization. A recent analysis identified 2029 as the highest-risk year for the AI bubble.

“There’s a clock in terms of the data center monetization and financing and how long it takes to build data centers,” Vellante said. “We know anybody who can sell GPUs is making money but the enterprises aren’t yet self-funding. I had said that by 2026, this year, you’re going to start to see clear evidence of monetization in the enterprise. I think you see it, but you’re seeing it within tech companies.”

Tech companies are applying AI more effectively, according to Vellante, which should not come as a surprise. He thinks the tech titans are in a solid position while neoclouds are taking on a greater share of risk by pioneering a new software model, although not all of them will make it in the long term.

A GPU-based AI economy will shift in the next several years, Furrier believes, which could lead to surprising winners and losers.

“Supermicro [Inc.], good numbers, [Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Arista Networks, Marvell Technology Inc.],” he noted. “My take is this: the infrastructure is evolving beyond GPU-centric computing. Networking, optics, memory, storage, power efficiency. System-level architecture is becoming the strategic advantage, and those bottlenecks are being solved by the companies I just mentioned. You saw the news that Marvell closed a $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum.”

The stock market plunge shows that not everyone is going to make it through the AI era’s eventual slowdown. Public opinion on data centers is mixed, to say the least, so companies will need to establish a foothold in the developing system of AI intelligence to remain competitive.

“Neoclouds like CoreWeave are going to make it through,” Vellante said. “They’re the first movers and they’ve got some quality advantages but they’re going to go through some pain. Hyperscalers are like an ATM. They could dial it down at any point in time … but right now it’s all about growth, it’s about footprint, it’s about market share.”

Who owns the “system of intelligence”? This layer, which will bridge the gap between intelligent agents and the data systems they depend on, appears to still be in play. Palantir Technologies Inc. has the ontology that could give it the edge, while Snowflake Inc. and Databricks Inc. are still developing the operational systems — though Vellante sees the latter as having one of the best strategies.

“You need determinism to own that system of intelligence,” Vellante said. “So I think it’s wide open. Right now, I think Ali Ghodsi [chief executive officer of Databricks] has the best vision. He’s going after the client surface, he’s going after the system of intelligence, he’s going after the governance catalog, he’s going after the agent action layer, and he’s partnering … with all the frontier model vendors. Whether or not they can pull it off, we’ll see.”

Frontier models are the “wild card,” as Vellante puts it, but at the moment, all the tech companies are trying to get a slice of the pie. Despite the recent market shakeups, Furrier sees AI-native enterprises as the ultimate result of this current period of growth.

“The AI-native enterprise or businesses is going to be the model,” Furrier said. “Everybody wins in that one. Compute providers, hyperscalers, the data platforms that are on the right side, and the application companies, which are basically going to be agentic. That’s going to be the winners on the profit concentration. The control point … it’s not going to be the models, it’s going to be data and context, and the agents will be the proof point.”

Tom Lee, investor and entrepreneur Dan Ives, technology analyst Frank Slootman, former chairman of the board of directors at Snowflake Inc. Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and chief executive officer of Databricks John Roese, global CTO and chief AI officer of Dell Technologies Lisa Su, chair and CEO of AMD Michael Dell, chairman and CEO of Dell Technologies George Gilbert, principal analyst at theCUBE Research Geoffrey Moore, principal at Geoffrey Moore Consulting Rob Hof, editor-in-chief at SiliconANGLE Media Stu Miniman, senior director of market insights, hybrid platforms, at Red Hat

#5516. What View Homes’ rebrand says about Gandhi’s operating overhaul

View Homes is consolidating its regional brands into a single identity as CEO Natasha Gandhi works to standardize operating practices and data systems. The company is expanding in Colorado and assessing how Hunt’s new Strata platform could support land strategy.  AI Summary

Seven months into her effort to transform View Homes from a loose collection of regional builders into a cohesive enterprise, CEO Natasha Gandhi has drawn a line between the company’s past and its ambitions.

A newly unified brand makes that promise visible. Now Gandhi and her team must overdeliver on it.

View Homes announced Monday a new corporate brand identity, unifying its formerly distinct Aspen View, Desert View, Horizon View and View Homes operations under one name. The change spans five divisions across Colorado, New Mexico and Texas and marks a milestone in the operational transformation Gandhi began after becoming CEO in March 2026.

The announcement also comes one week after View’s parent, Hunt Companies, joined with global investment manager Wafra to launch Strata Land Partners, a new land-financing platform led by former Landsea Homes president Michael Forsum. Together, these developments offer a clearer view of Hunt’s expanding ambitions in U.S. residential construction and development.

In an exclusive interview with HousingWire TBD, Gandhi said the branding initiative is part of a broader effort to prepare View for growth, strengthen operating standards, and compete across more markets and homebuyer segments.

“We want to be a premium builder, and by premium, it’s not that we’re unaffordable,” Gandhi said. “It just means that we want to be the best in every price point that we’re out there, we want to be the best in every market that we build in.”

Hunt acquired full ownership of View Homes in 2025, inheriting an established 35-year-old homebuilding business whose regional operations had developed distinct identities, systems and operating practices.

When Gandhi arrived in March, she found an organization with strong local relationships and experienced teams, but lacking the consistent management processes, reporting systems, and enterprise infrastructure needed to support the growth Hunt envisioned.

As The Builder’s Daily reported in October, Gandhi’s initial work focused on leadership changes, clearer accountability, more disciplined sales concessions, selective land investment, and a comprehensive review of enterprise technology.

The new branding establishes four standards intended to apply across the organization: exceptional customer experience, people-first leadership, design-forward homes, and premium quality across price points.

“I felt like previously, we had different standards in different markets, but now with this new brand, it really sets the stage,” Gandhi said. “These four pillars are something that is now going to be operationally executed in all our markets.”

The challenge is to translate those commitments into consistent performance without compromising the local knowledge and customer relationships that have made View’s regional businesses successful.

For a multiregional homebuilder, Gandhi notes, that means more than consistent signage and marketing. It requires shared expectations for product quality, customer service, sales execution, and management accountability, supported by reliable information and operating systems.

Gandhi is candid that the transformation remains unfinished. “This is just the start of our growth journey,” she said. “I will tell you, we’re not there yet, but we’re on the path of getting there.”

The branding initiative has prompted further scrutiny of the operational capabilities needed to support the company’s ambitions to up its game. Gandhi acknowledged that View’s enterprise resource planning systems and website are not yet up to par.

A builder seeking to expand across markets needs timely, consistent information on sales, margins, construction costs, inventory, and land commitments. Without it, management cannot easily compare performance across divisions or make informed decisions about capital allocation.

Gandhi previously outlined a 12-to-18-month enterprise technology implementation, along with efforts to standardize sales concessions and improve the quality of operating data. Those initiatives remain important to the company’s ability to scale.

View has also raised the bar in its home merchandising across markets and is developing products designed to reach beyond its traditional entry-level customer base. The objective is to preserve affordability where that remains the market opportunity while broadening View’s appeal to move-up buyers and customers seeking greater design and product differentiation.

The transformation is unfolding amid difficult housing economics. Slower sales, persistent affordability pressures, and costly incentives continue to strain builder margins, while land acquisition and development require substantial capital commitments long before homes generate revenue.

Hunt’s ownership gives View access to a larger real estate investment organization and a longer-term investment perspective. Its recent partnership with Wafra to establish Strata Land Partners adds another potentially valuable capability.

Strata launched with projects comprising approximately 1,300 single-family lots and a mandate to provide flexible land-financing solutions for public and private homebuilders and developers nationwide. Forsum has described the platform as a capital partner “built by builders, for builders,” emphasizing the need to understand the operational risks and financial requirements of homebuilding businesses.

Gandhi confirmed that View and Strata are already discussing opportunities to work together.

“We are actually already exploring opportunities to where Strata and [View] can partner together,” she said. “There’s definitely opportunity and conversations already in place.”

She did not identify specific transactions or financing structures under review.

Still, the potential relationship illustrates how Hunt’s residential investments could create complementary advantages. View brings homebuilding operations, local market relationships, and demand for future lots. Strata brings a platform designed to finance land acquisition and development while managing builders’ capital exposure.

Whether those capabilities translate into direct financial or operational advantages for View will depend on the transactions and terms the companies ultimately pursue. Strata’s mandate extends well beyond Hunt-owned businesses.

Gandhi said she has assembled the leadership team she believes can execute View’s next phase, including experienced executives recruited during the restructuring process.

“It’s your people that get you the results,” she said. “It’s your people that help you navigate a tough market.”

That leadership investment comes as View prepares to expand into Sterling Ranch, a master-planned community in Douglas County, Colorado, near Denver.

View currently operates in Northern Colorado, Colorado Springs, and Las Cruces, El Paso, and San Antonio. Sterling Ranch gives the company an opportunity to establish a stronger presence in the Denver metropolitan market, where Gandhi sees additional growth opportunities.

She said View is close to completing other land transactions in the Denver area and is pursuing opportunities in additional master-planned communities.

The expansion also offers an early test of the unified brand’s positioning. View intends to compete as a premium regional builder while maintaining a product range that serves buyers across price points.

Gandhi’s transformation is underway as many homebuilders protect cash, reduce land commitments, and prepare for the possibility that difficult conditions could persist through 2027 and 2028. View must balance those immediate pressures with Hunt’s longer-term objective of building a substantially larger homebuilding enterprise.

The company is not simply adding communities to its existing business. Gandhi is working to establish the leadership, systems, product standards, and capital discipline needed to support growth without replicating the fragmented operating structure she inherited.

“My goal, Hunt’s goal, is for View to grow into a premium regional builder,” Gandhi said. “I would like to see View be among the top 50, top 25 home builders in the next five years.”

Achieving that scale will require more than additional land and investment capital. View must demonstrate that its five divisions can operate consistently, protect margins amid changing market conditions, and deliver – or exceed – the customer experience its new brand promises.

#5515. Securitize to Acquire River One, Connecting Stablecoin Capital to the $6 Trillion Asset-Backed Finance Market

Acquisition will add institutional warehouse financing capabilities to Securitize's tokenization infrastructure, creating new opportunities to finance real-world assets

MIAMI, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Securitize Corp. (NYSE: SECZ), the leading platform for tokenized assets, today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire River Credit Labs Inc. ("River One"), an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets.

Upon closing, the acquisition will add a new financing layer to Securitize's platform, expanding its capabilities beyond the issuance and servicing of tokenized assets to include asset-backed lending. By combining Securitize's tokenization infrastructure with River One's warehouse financing technology, the companies aim to enable institutions to bring financial assets onchain and access financing against those assets through an integrated platform.

Acquisition will add new financing layer to Securitize's platform expanding capabilities to include asset-backed lending

The transaction positions Securitize to enter the $6 trillion global private asset-backed finance market, where banks, private credit funds and specialty lenders provide capital to businesses backed by portfolios of income-generating assets. River One focuses on providing institutional-quality financing solutions to creditworthy borrowers, combining rigorous AI-based underwriting with flexible financing structures and access to new sources of capital.

The acquisition comes as the global stablecoin market has grown to approximately $321 billion, creating new opportunities to put digital capital to work in the real economy. At the same time, demand for asset-backed financing continues to expand, with KKR estimating that the global private asset-backed finance market could grow from $6 trillion to $9.2 trillion by 2029.

"Credit is one of the most exciting emerging asset classes for blockchain-based financial markets, and acquiring River One represents an important step in expanding our business into this space," said Carlos Domingo, Chairman and CEO of Securitize. "River One brings a talented team, deep expertise in asset-backed financing and blockchain technology that will allow us to participate in asset origination and lending markets. This opens up a significant new addressable market for Securitize, with opportunities for higher-value services, additional revenue streams and greater monetization across our platform."

River One was incubated by Framework Ventures, with investment backing from both Framework Ventures and Maple Finance.

Founded in New York in 2025, River One specializes in warehouse financing backed by portfolios of income-generating assets, including small business loans, receivables and other collateral. Warehouse facilities provide lenders and other loan originators with capital to fund loans as they are originated.

River One's platform brings AI powered origination capabilities and structuring, facility setup, borrowing-base reporting, collateral monitoring and funding operations together in a single system, giving lenders and borrowers a shared, real-time view of their financing positions. Its technology is designed to streamline the management of warehouse credit facilities while combining traditional underwriting and legal protections with blockchain-based financial infrastructure.

"Asset-backed financing is a critical part of the financial system, but the infrastructure supporting it has significant room for innovation," said Braham Mehta, Co-Founder and CEO of River One. "We built River One to bring modern AI and blockchain technology and new sources of capital to institutional lending while maintaining the credit discipline and protections these markets require. Joining Securitize gives us the opportunity to bring this approach to a much larger market."

River One is developing relationships with capital providers in the stablecoin ecosystem to support the financing of high-quality, income-generating assets. Its model is designed to maintain traditional credit underwriting standards and legal protections, including special-purpose vehicles designed to be bankruptcy-remote, collateral requirements and ongoing portfolio monitoring, while using blockchain technology to improve financing efficiency.

The acquisition is expected to expand Securitize's addressable market and create additional revenue opportunities from institutional financing activity, connecting its existing tokenization infrastructure with River One's credit capabilities.

The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions.

Securitize Corp. (NYSE: SECZ), the leading platform for tokenized assets with approximately $5B in AUM as of September 2026, is bringing the world onchain through tokenized funds in partnership with top-tier asset managers such as Apollo, BlackRock, BNY, Hamilton Lane, KKR, VanEck and others. It is the only company operating regulated digital-securities infrastructure in both the U.S. and EU, and has been named to the Forbes 2026 Fintech 50 and CNBC World's Top Fintech Companies 2026 lists.

River One is a New York-based institutional asset-backed financing platform focused on connecting stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Its technology supports the origination, structuring and management of warehouse credit facilities, including borrowing-base reporting, collateral monitoring and funding operations, with the goal of expanding access to financing for financial institutions, fintech lenders and asset originators.

This press release contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the federal securities laws, including statements regarding the expected timing and completion of Securitize's proposed acquisition of River One; the anticipated benefits of the transaction; the integration of River One's technology and personnel; Securitize's expansion into asset-backed financing and lending markets; potential products, services, customers, financing activity, revenue opportunities and addressable markets; and expectations regarding stablecoins, tokenization and asset-backed finance.

Forward-looking statements are based on current expectations, estimates and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. These risks include, among others, the possibility that closing conditions may not be satisfied; that the transaction may be delayed or may not close; difficulties integrating River One's technology, operations or personnel; the early-stage nature of River One's business and technology; the ability to establish relationships with capital providers and borrowers; credit, liquidity, counterparty, technology, cybersecurity, regulatory and market risks; and the other risks described in Securitize's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Readers should not place undue reliance on these forward-looking statements, which speak only as of the date of this release. Securitize undertakes no obligation to update these statements except as required by law.

KKR and Integer Advisors estimates based on data available as of March 31, 2024. The estimate represents private financial assets originated and held by non-banks globally and excludes certain securitized, government-related and secondary-market assets. The $9.2 trillion figure is a KKR estimate for 2029 and is not a prediction by Securitize. Forecasts are inherently uncertain.

#5514. Hollywood Prediction Market Faces Insider Scare: James Bond Casting Bets Shift

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hollywood studios are tightening restrictions on employees betting on prediction market after suspicious activity surrounding the next James Bond casting decision. The prediction market controversy intensified after a platform temporarily pulled its market following a sudden wave of bets backing Callum Turner.

The Hollywood Reporter reported that studios and production companies have been quietly warning employees against wagering on confidential industry information. The restrictions cover casting decisions, movie release dates, and studio earnings. At least one company has reportedly established an anonymous hotline for reporting suspected insider betting.

THR has learned studios and production companies have been quietly issuing new guidelines to employees warning them not to engage in prediction market betting.• The warnings prohibit employees from placing bets on news events like studio earnings, casting, or even release… pic.twitter.com/JbiovSwZC9

The crackdown follows growing interest in entertainment contracts on platforms such as Polymarket and Kalshi. Employees could potentially turn confidential production information into profits before announcements reach the public. They are also being warned against passing information to friends or relatives who could place bets on their behalf.

A prediction market platform temporarily suspended its next James Bond casting market after a sudden wave of sharp money pushed Callum Turner ahead of longtime favorite Jack Lowden. The movement raised concerns that traders might have received information about the casting decision before an official announcement.

Turner’s odds had already improved following casting rumors and reports of screen tests. However, the sudden betting activity attracted additional attention, particularly because Amazon MGM Studios has yet to announce its next 007.

Entertainment contracts can cover award winners, reality television eliminations, celebrity appearances, and confidential production developments. The potential for insider betting is particularly concerning when employees have access to information that ordinary participants cannot obtain.

#5513. Trump strikes a softer note on immigration; builders need proof

Trump said immigration policy may be too tough and suggested a deal for long-term undocumented workers. Administration signals remain mixed as ICE raids and arrest targets pressure builders ahead of 2027.  AI Summary

On Sunday, President Donald Trump indicated that he is open to negotiating an immigration deal with the incoming Democratic Congress. However, despite softening post-election rhetoric, the Trump administration appears to be sending mixed signals on immigration, clouding the outlook for any potential bipartisan agreement.

The stakes of the nation’s highly contentious immigration debate remain high for homebuilders. After a surge in job site raids by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) this summer and fall, many homebuilders say their workers, including those in the country legally, were swept up in enforcement actions.

Whether a bipartisan immigration deal materializes remains an open and pressing question for the numerous builders facing ongoing job site disruptions.

Speaking to CBS News’ 60 Minutes on Sunday, President Trump suggested his administration’s immigration policies “might be too tough” and may have contributed to last week’s election outcome.

“When you go into a hotel…and you have a woman that’s worked there as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress – a lot of good things, great jobs – and all of a sudden, they’re being taken out of the country. It’s tough. It’s a tough thing,” Trump said.

Trump added that it may be “doable” to reach an agreement allowing undocumented workers who have lived in the U.S. for many years, construction workers among them, to legally remain in the country.

“Get the killers out. Get the rapists out. Get all the rough ones out. Get the drug dealers out, but let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” Trump suggested.

It’s unclear whether Trump’s softer rhetoric will translate into a bipartisan immigration deal. However, his administration’s decision to promote Stephen Miller, a longtime immigration hardliner, to White House Chief of Staff suggests an agreement may be less likely than Trump implied in his CBS News interview.

And in a post on Sunday, the Official White House Rapid Response account, in a post on X, denied that Trump will push for an amnesty deal with Democrats.

However, Trump has at times shown a willingness to soften his stance on immigration, at least briefly. In June 2025, the Trump administration momentarily directed ICE to pause job site raids in sectors like agriculture, hospitality and restaurants after facing blowback from business leaders worried about staffing shortages.

Within days, however, the administration reversed course. It later set a target of 3,000 ICE arrests per day, leading to a record number of immigration arrests in recent months.

Trump has also helped kill a bipartisan deal before. In early 2024, ahead of the presidential election, he urged Republicans to vote against a Senate border package introduced by Sen. James Lankford (R-OK) that would have tightened asylum requirements, ended releases of migrants into U.S. communities while they await hearings, and let the president close the border when asylum claims surged. The bill ultimately failed.

Some homebuilding organizations, like the National Association of Home Builders, now have their eyes on a different bipartisan measure, the Dignity Act, which would allow certain undocumented workers to remain in the U.S. without citizenship. Trump’s words signaled openness to such a proposal, but the administration’s actions since the election suggest otherwise.

Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, laid out in a post-midterms election post on X that the administration may be open to changing its approach to immigration, with less room for negotiation.

“Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement – by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” Vance wrote.

For homebuilders, immigration policy and its impact on the construction labor pool remains among the biggest policy questions heading into 2027. However, history suggests that a bipartisan deal may be a heavy lift, as Washington hasn’t passed comprehensive immigration reform since 1986, under President Reagan.

Whether Washington breaks its four-decade drought on immigration reform, and whether enforcement eases on job sites, remains a key policy wild card to watch in 2027.

#5512. Real Estate Expert Matt Nuzie Explains Buying and Selling a Home at the Same Time

The article explains how homeowners can plan their finances, decide whether to buy or sell first, and coordinate closing dates when moving from one home to the next.

TRUMBULL, Conn., Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ --

How can homeowners manage buying and selling a home at the same time? A HelloNation article provides the answer, featuring insights from Matt Nuzie, Real Estate Expert with REMAX Right Choice in Trumbull, Connecticut. The newly published article explains how financial planning, mortgage options, and closing dates affect both sides of the move.

The article explains that selling your current home first gives homeowners certainty. Once the sale closes, they know exactly what they have for a down payment and a price range.

Selling first also removes the risk of carrying two homes. The trade-off is that homeowners may need temporary housing, storage, or two moves.

Buying a new home first lets homeowners move on their own schedule. The article notes that it can mean covering two mortgage payments, property taxes, insurance, and utilities, so a conversation with a lender should come before any offer.

How Do Mortgage Options Affect Buying and Selling?

According to the article, mortgage options often decide the order. Some buyers need the equity from their current home for a down payment, while others qualify for financing that lets them buy before selling.

Matt Nuzie recommends reviewing income, savings, and the current mortgage with a lender before touring homes.  A home sale contingency makes a purchase dependent on selling the buyer's current home. It offers protection, but many sellers prefer offers without one when they have several to choose from.

Matt Nuzie notes that scheduling both closings close together lets homeowners move directly from one home to the next.

Closings can be delayed for ordinary reasons, such as a lender's request for documents or an inspection issue, so building in some breathing room is wise.

A rent-back agreement can let sellers stay in the home for an agreed period after closing. Short-term temporary housing is another option when the dates don't line up.

How Can Homeowners Prepare for Unexpected Costs?

The article recommends starting early on cleaning, small repairs, and listing photos, since they often take longer than expected.

Moving, storage, repairs, and temporary housing can add up quickly, so setting aside extra savings helps.

Matt Nuzie also emphasizes keeping the real estate agent, lender, and attorney informed of deadlines, and reading contract terms closely before signing.

How to Buy and Sell a Home at the Same Time features insights from Matt Nuzie, Real Estate Expert of Trumbull, Connecticut, in HelloNation.

Is It Better to Buy or Sell a Home First?

According to Matt Nuzie, it depends on your finances, your moving plans, and the local real estate market. Selling first brings financial certainty, while buying first offers more flexibility with the move.

Matt Nuzie explains through insights featured in the article that a home sale contingency makes a purchase dependent on selling an existing home. It offers protection, though many sellers prefer offers without one.

Can You Close on Two Homes at the Same Time?

The article explains that homeowners can schedule both closings close together. Financing or inspection delays can still shift the timing, so some cushion is wise.

What Happens if Closing Dates Do Not Match?

Based on insights from Matt Nuzie, Real Estate Expert of Trumbull, Connecticut, homeowners may consider a rent-back agreement or short-term temporary housing. Both can provide extra time between transactions.

#5511. Century Communities names Jim Francescon as president

Century Communities Inc. announced that Jim Francescon, currently executive vice president of corporate operations, will be promoted to president effective Jan. 1, 2027. In his new position, Jim will oversee homebuilding operations, land and related corporate functions, building on his work leading recent acquisitions in Texas and Tennessee.   AI Summary

Century Communities Inc. (NYSE: CCS) announced on Monday that Jim Francescon has been promoted to president, effective Jan. 1, 2027, as part of the company’s long-term succession planning process.

The company, ranked 13th by sales volume in the HousingWire Homebuilder Rankings, said Dale Francescon will continue to serve as executive chairman. Rob Francescon, who currently serves as chief executive officer and president, will remain CEO.

As president, Jim Francescon will oversee Century Communities’ homebuilding operations, land and related corporate functions and will help drive the company’s strategy and growth, according to the announcement.

“Today’s announcement reflects the implementation of a succession plan that our Board, Rob, and I have been planning and executing over the past two years,” Dale Francescon, executive chairman of Century Communities, said in a statement. “We have been very thoughtful in how we have approached succession, with the goal of best positioning Century for long-term alignment with shareholders, success and growth.”

“Jim has played an integral role in shaping our strategic direction and our growth into one of the largest homebuilders in the country, including leading our recent acquisitions that have deepened our footprint and strengthened our platform,” Rob Francescon, CEO of Century Communities, said. “I look forward to continuing to work closely with Jim and our entire executive team as we position Century for continued success.”

Jim Francescon said he is “honored to take on this role and grateful to our Board, Dale and Rob for their confidence.”

“We have built a strong operating platform and a talented team, and I am excited about the opportunities ahead as we continue to grow and deliver on our promise of A Home for Every Dream®,” he said.

Francescon joined Century Communities in 2019 and most recently served as executive vice president, corporate operations, overseeing much of the company’s corporate operations, including homebuilding, land, strategy, business development, and mergers and acquisitions.

In that role, he led the company’s acquisition strategy, including recent acquisitions of HistoryMaker Homes, Anglia Homes and Landmark Homes of Tennessee, which expanded Century’s presence in Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Nashville, respectively.

Before serving as executive vice president, Francescon was president of Century Living, the company’s multifamily platform, and earlier served as corporate vice president. Prior to joining Century, he worked in private equity at GoldPoint Partners, a subsidiary of New York Life Investments, and in investment banking at J.P. Morgan Securities LLC.

He holds a Bachelor of Science in business administration with a concentration in finance and real estate and a Master of Science in finance from the University of Denver. Francescon also serves as a trustee of the University of Denver, Children’s Hospital Colorado Foundation and ACE Scholarships Colorado.

#5509. Cisco research: Trust, not technology, is now the speed limit on enterprise AI

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For several years, the conversation about enterprise artificial intelligence has focused on capability: which model is smartest and which GPU is fastest. That made sense when technology was the constraint.

It isn’t anymore. AI can now do far more than most organizations will allow, and the gap is trust.

That’s the core finding of “Permission to Scale: The Critical Role of Trust in Successful AI Adoption,” new research released today at Cisco Systems Inc.’s Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne. Authored by independent researcher Brad Howarth, the study draws on data from 25 Australian organizations.

At Cisco Live APJC, Cisco hosted a press panel to discuss the report. The panel, moderated by Howarth, featured a number of corporate leaders from companies that participated in the report, including Carl Solder, chief technology officer of Cisco ANZ (far left); Anna Tosky, chief people officer at Elmo Software (second from left); Chris Locke, CTO at Flight Center Travel Group (third from left); Naz Wilson, group culture and enablement manager at Funlab (third from right); and Lucio Ribeiro, chief AI officer at TBWA Australia (second from right).

Though a sample size of 25 is small, the results align with conversations I’ve had with corporate leadership. I appreciated the panel’s mix of technologies, human resources and cultural leadership. I also valued the mix of roles, as the biggest barrier to scaling AI isn’t technical but people-related.

Australia makes an interesting test case. According to University of Melbourne and KPMG research cited in the report, half of Australians use AI regularly, but only 36% trust it, and just 30% believe its benefits outweigh its risks. That’s the lowest among 47 countries surveyed. If you can build trust in AI in Australia, that work will scale globally. In the press release, Stefan Leitl, vice president and general manager of Cisco Australia and New Zealand, discussed the benefits of winning over this region: “It’s a playbook that travels well beyond Australia.”

Solder noted that among the six pillars in Cisco’s AI Readiness Index, chief information officers and CTOs gravitate toward what they know, namely infrastructure and data, and leave culture for others. He described a customer that invested in infrastructure, governance, data and information technology skills but “didn’t focus on the culture. And they found that there was a big pushback from their employees and customers on using the toolsets they’ve invested in.”

This is something I’ve seen repeatedly: Companies spend millions on AI platforms only to see utilization remain tepid. Howarth discussed an adoption “flywheel” in which successful use creates evidence, evidence builds trust and trust enables broader use. Companies sit around waiting for trust before deploying, and the evidence of trust must be something measurable.

Trust in AI needs to be established with realistic parameters. Many people reject AI after a single mistake, even though in most cases the error rate is much lower than that of people. This mirrors what the automotive industry went through when a Tesla accident would trigger a media storm. The reality is that Tesla’s Autopilot system experiences one crash for about every 7 million miles, compared with human drivers, who average about one crash every 1 million miles.

Perfection isn’t a realistic goal, but being faster and more accurate than others is. Users should understand this going into any kind of trial or proof of concept, as the expectation of perfection can erode trust.

Chris Locke offered a great example of an executive leading by example. The company’s 77-year-old founder, Graham “Skroo” Turner, uses AI every day. “He’s a big Anthropic Claude user,” Locke said. “This is also a guy who once said the internet wouldn’t catch on back in 2000. He may have gotten that one wrong, but he’s betting on AI catching on, so I think he gives us permission to play.”

Ribeiro outlined a more structured approach, describing trust as an equation built on four elements: ownership, competence, consistency and transparency. He was matter-of-fact about why asking a nervous workforce whether it wants AI doesn’t yield an accurate answer. “You never ask a barber if you need a haircut, as the answer is always yes.”

His alternative was honesty. Companies can’t promise to protect every job, but they can promise to make employees “the most prepared, trained, trusted person” if AI disrupts their role.

Funlab, where 79% of the workforce is 21 or younger, relies on peer learning. Its “AI Super Squad” convenes representatives from every department every four weeks. Wilson said early sessions simply clarified which tools were safe, because many employees’ real limitation was “just not knowing whether I am allowed to do certain things or not.”

The report’s central concept is calibrated trust. People need to know when to rely on AI, when to verify its outputs, and when a human must decide. Blindly trusting these systems and their outputs is a significant risk.

During the Q&A, I asked how companies protect against over-trust, especially in high-intensity jobs where people just take the answer and move on. Tosky was candid. “The AI slop. It’s real,” she said. “You ask the employee a question, prompt the AI system and then they send a report without looking at it, and it’s completely wrong. It’s 10 pages you now have to read.”

Elmo keeps a human in the loop on nearly everything, and she argued that the fix starts with redesigning the work. “It’s very unsexy, but start with the process itself, instead of just going, ‘OK, let’s throw a bunch of agents at it.'”

The report recommends that IT leaders adopt a specific practice: Stop treating log-ins as a proxy for trust, and track how often people challenge or override AI outputs. Usage shows people are clicking. Override rates show they’re thinking.

I also raised a contact center concern. AI automates the mundane tasks that served as cognitive breaks for agents, leaving them with nonstop, high-intensity work and higher churn. Tosky called it “AI brain fry” and suggested rethinking metrics and breaks. Wilson added that if AI absorbs routine work, employees lose the repetition that builds context and expertise. That’s a talent pipeline problem few companies are considering.

AI that drafts content is one thing; agents that act are another. Locke said Flight Centre now has agents handling a small subset of airline ticketing that was previously outsourced offshore, with security engaged from day one. He used AI to book his Uber to the event, but a return flight to Europe? “Not yet.”

Fewer than half of respondents are very or extremely confident that their foundations are ready for more autonomous AI, and more than half say their infrastructure needs upgrading. Cisco’s 2026 Relentless Defense report found that only 36% of Australian organizations apply consistent controls to AI agents and nonhuman identities. In the report, Lendi Group CTO Devesh Maheshwari described the target as “bounded autonomy, where the agent can act on your behalf but cannot go beyond the boundaries you have established.”

This is where Cisco can help its enterprise customers. Solder argues that trust must be enforced at the network and security layers. “Built into the network and security underneath, control stops being the brake and becomes the permission to move faster,” he said. Cisco is betting that its networking, security and Splunk portfolio will become the trust layer for agentic AI, and the report provides a business rationale for that bet.

As I stated above, the research is qualitative and aligns with what I hear from CIOs globally. My advice for IT leaders:

The AI winners won’t necessarily have the best models. They’ll have employees, boards and customers who trust the systems enough to let them do more. As Solder put it, “The leaders in our research aren’t scaling AI first. They’re scaling trust.”

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5508. HECM endorsements rebound in October but stay near decade low

Federally insured reverse mortgage activity improved modestly in October 2026, with HECM endorsements rising 11% from September to 1,995, according to Reverse Market Insight and HECMWorld.com. The market remains near a 10-year low and slightly behind last year’s pace, with Finance of America, Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha dominating volume.   AI Summary

The federally insured reverse mortgage market posted a rebound in October, but activity remained at historically low levels compared to the past decade, according to data compiled by Reverse Market Insight (RMI) and published Friday by HECMWorld.com.

Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) endorsements rose to 1,995 in October, an 11% increase from September and the highest level in three months, the data shows. But even with the gain, this was the lowest figure for the month of October in at least 10 years.

Year to date, endorsements are about 3.19% below last year’s level — but comparisons are complicated by the federal government shutdown in October 2025, which disrupted activity and reporting.

Finance of America Reverse (FOA) remained the top HECM lender in October with 460 endorsements, followed by Longbridge Financial with 362 and Mutual of Omaha Mortgage with 332. Goodlife Home Loans posted 110 endorsements and Fairway Home Mortgage recorded 67.

Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha switched positions from September, and Goodlife jumped three spots by originating 62 more HECMs compared to the prior month. The top three lenders accounted for about 63% of all HECM endorsements in October, underscoring how concentrated the reverse mortgage business has become.

The number of active lenders with more than one HECM endorsement improved, rising to 75 in October from 63 in September.

From January through October, FOA widened its lead with 4,398 endorsements. Mutual of Omaha ranked second with 4,041, followed by Longbridge at 3,513, Goodlife at 916 and South River Mortgage at 692.

While endorsements increased, securitization volume moved in the opposite direction. HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities (HMBS) issuance in October was down 16% from September.

New View Advisors, citing its analysis of data from Ginnie Mae and private sources, reported that October HMBS issuance totaled $419 million, a decline of $27 million from September. There were 61 pools issued in October, nine fewer than in September.

FOA led all issuers in October with $180 million in HMBS issuance, up from $175 million in September. Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha saw month-over-month declines, issuing $116 million and $76 million, respectively.

First-participation pool production dropped to $238 million in October, down $28 million from September and $97 million from October 2025. New View said issuers “continue to struggle with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%.”

From January to October, FOA was the top first-participation HMBS issuer with $1.01 billion of issuance, according to New View. Longbridge followed at $863 million and Mutual of Omaha at $593 million.

In October, the 61 HMBS pools consisted of 14 first-participation pools and 47 tail pools. New View also highlighted the ongoing use of very small pools as 18 of the October pools had an aggregate size below $1 million, totaling $10.8 million of unpaid principal balance that might not otherwise have been issued.

#5506. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5505. California voters reject measure to shred environmental red tape

California voters voted down Proposition 45, which sought to speed CEQA environmental reviews through standardized deadlines and faster court timelines. The measure lost 56% to 44% in unofficial returns, and the streamlining fight is expected to return to the Legislature.  AI Summary

California voters have rejected a ballot measure to speed environmental review of housing and other projects.

Proposition 45 would have consolidated a patchwork of legislative fixes to the California Environmental Quality Act, aimed largely at reducing a costly hurdle to building housing. The Associated Press called the race over the weekend, though the state is still counting votes. Unofficial returns showed about 56% of voters opposed and 44% in favor, a spread too large to overcome with the remaining votes.

It failed decisively across populous coastal counties, where housing affordability is a pressing concern. Voters in Santa Cruz, Marin and Sonoma counties rejected the measure by the widest margins.

Opponents tied the measure to data center development, an influential argument in midterm races nationwide.

“Californians have sent a clear message to corporate developers, utilities and data center builders that they will not stand for a broad assault at the ballot box on state law protecting our air, water and natural resources,” the Vote No on Prop 45 campaign released in a statement.

Proponents dubbed that an inaccurate scare tactic.

“The opposition relentlessly lied, falsely claiming that Prop 45 covered data centers when non-partisan experts agreed it did not – and used smokestack images and scare tactics about air and water pollution when the ‘essential projects’ included in Prop 45 did not include smokestack industries and also excluded mining, port, and other controversial projects,” Jennifer Hernandez, who leads Holland & Knight’s West Coast land-use and environmental group, told HousingWire TBD.

Opponents also countered the claim that the measure would help create affordable housing. They cited housing groups that urged a no vote or declined to endorse. Abundant Housing LA and California YIMBY, both of which endorsed L.A. Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, did not endorse the measure.

Opponents included the California Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters and the American Lung Association. Sierra Club California and the California Federation of Labor Unions also opposed it.

The California Chamber of Commerce sponsored the measure, with backing from home-builder groups and some affordable housing advocates.

“We were outspent but not outgunned, thanks to a broad bipartisan coalition that understood that Californians know we can have progress and safeguard our environment at the same time,” the campaign noted in its statement.

Had it passed, the measure would have capped full environmental impact reports at 365 business days. Court challenges would have faced a 270-day limit.

Covered “essential” projects included housing, water, energy, schools, health facilities and transportation. Applicants could have chosen the new procedures or the existing ones.

The Legislative Analyst’s Office said the measure could cost local governments up to $100 million a year at first. Long-term financial effects were unclear. A Chamber-commissioned analysis projected $1.5 billion in savings and added revenue over 10 years.

Prop. 45 followed a run of legislative changes that limited CEQA reviews of housing proposals. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 130 and Senate Bill 131 in 2025. They exempted qualifying infill housing from CEQA and narrowed review for some projects falling short of an exemption.

A newer round of bills signed this fall targets more permitting delays. Some shield specific developments from further CEQA challenges. One is a major mixed-use development in San Diego.

Backers argued those fixes helped only some projects. They said project-specific exemptions left other developments exposed to years of delay. Prop. 45 would have applied common deadlines to all eligible projects.

Supporters said predictable timelines would help California build homes and the infrastructure that serves them. They said CEQA lawsuits add tens of millions of dollars in costs, and thwart efforts to increase housing supply by escalating entitlement risk. They also argued that the measure could cut delays by two to 10 years.

“Not-in-my-backyard” and environmental groups have long sued local governments under CEQA. Those suits typically argue agencies did not properly handle environmental impact reviews.

A study by Hernandez and other researchers reviewed 498 CEQA appellate decisions from 2013 through 2023. Agencies prevailed in 75%. But the study said prolonged litigation still stalls financing and raises costs. It covers appellate decisions only and predates the 2025 reforms.

Opponents said the 2025 reforms already addressed much of CEQA’s housing problem. They said Prop. 45 would cap public-comment periods, narrow tribal consultation and limit judicial review. They also argued that affordability was being used as cover for a developer advantage.

Critics said “essential” was defined so broadly that it could fast-track freeways, power plants and pipelines.

The fight to streamline CEQA may now shift back to the Legislature and a new governor.

“We know this fight is not over,” the No on Prop 45 campaign wrote in its statement.

“The good news is that many millions of Californians voted for Prop 45, and do want timely, accountable, and predictable outcomes in CEQA,” Hernandez said. “Our legislative supporters saw the dirty trick campaign tactics unfold, and now have the opportunity to adopt these important CEQA reforms for the ‘essential projects’ that California needs to restore affordability to our state.”

#5504. Lafayette Square Institute and the Center for USA Lending Launch Federal Credit Lab Platform

Federal Credit Lab provides publicly available data visualizations and analysis on the allocation of federal credit across the U.S. economy.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, Lafayette Square Institute and the Center for USA Lending launched the Federal Credit Lab, a publicly available data and insights platform providing data and analysis of the U.S. government credit portfolio to generate actionable insights for policymakers, program administrators, researchers, and the public.

The United States government is one of the largest lenders in the world. Its portfolio contains over $5 trillion in cumulative outstanding loans and loan guarantees. In Fiscal Year 2026 alone, Congress authorized nearly $1 trillion in new loan and loan guarantees spanning over 100 programs and 20 federal agencies.

Federal Credit Lab is a joint initiative of two nonprofit organizations, the Lafayette Square Institute and the Center for USA Lending, aimed at making this portfolio data more readily accessible to inform better program assessment, delivery, budgeting, and design.

"Federal credit is one of the most powerful and least understood sets of tools by which policymakers can mobilize private capital to address national challenges," said Jack Moriarty, Executive Director of Lafayette Square Institute. "Our objective in building Federal Credit Lab with our partners at the Center for USA Lending is to enhance our collective understanding of this toolkit to inform the next generation of industrial policy and the allocation of capital to the people and places that need it."

"Modern systems and better information lead to better policy. The Federal Credit Lab puts that premise into practice. It is a platform that makes the government's lending enterprise substantially more visible, accessible, and accountable. We see this as a foundation, one we hope to build on in partnership with federal credit agencies," said Doug Criscitello, Executive Director of the Center for USA Lending.

"By applying analytics to the complex workflows across the federal credit portfolio, Lafayette Square Institute and the Center for USA Lending are creating conditions for government and capital markets to better serve workers and communities in every zip code," said Damien Dwin, Founder and CEO of Lafayette Square and Board member of Lafayette Square Institute.

"The Federal Credit Lab platform aspires to make the world of federal credit accessible to a much wider audience of stakeholders by centralizing and unifying a previously disparate set of data sources," said Laura Hohenberger, Senior Associate for Data Analytics and Policy at Lafayette Square Institute.

The launch of the Federal Credit Lab featured a joint event in Washington, D.C. that included a platform demo and expert speakers. Additional programming on select thematic areas in the federal credit portfolio is slated throughout 2027. Lafayette Square Institute and the Center for USA Lending invite public feedback on applied research questions for future analysis.

About Lafayette Square Institute Lafayette Square Institute (LSI) is a nonprofit policy and data analytics platform committed to aligning private capital with the public interest. Through deep bipartisan relationships, innovative finance tools, and data analysis, LSI mobilizes investment in the people and places that need it.

About Center for USA Lending The Center for USA Lending is a nonpartisan organization advancing a modern, effective credit ecosystem. It connects public and private stakeholders, elevates borrower needs, and promotes the use of modern technology to ensure access to capital for the borrowers federal credit is intended to serve.

#5503. Dorsata, Inc. Notifies Patients of Metabase Data Security Incident

CHARLOTTESVILLE, Va., Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Dorsata, Inc. has become aware of a data security incident involving the Metabase third-party software it uses that may have involved the protected health information belonging to patients. Dorsata is sending letters to potentially involved individuals to notify them about this incident and provide resources to assist them.

On or about August 12, 2026, Dorsata received a notice that the Metabase business intelligence software it uses contained a security vulnerability. They immediately patched the software and began an investigation with the assistance of independent cybersecurity experts. The investigation determined the Metabase security vulnerability allowed unauthorized access to its database platform that stores medical information related to patients of Dorsata's healthcare provider partners between August 10, 2026 and August 12, 2026. Dorsata then reviewed the data involved in the incident to identify the individuals whose information may have been involved. Please note that there is no evidence of the misuse, or attempted misuse, of any potentially impacted information.

On October 21, 2026, Dorsata began sending notification letters to the individuals potentially involved in this incident providing them information about what happened and steps they can take to protect their information.

Based on the investigation of the incident, the following personal and protected health information may have been involved in the incident: name, address, patient ID, date of birth, vitals data, treatment information, treatment location, provider name, vaccines, medications, health insurance information, and patients' medical history contained in a patient's medical records. Social security numbers, driver's license number, and financial information were not involved.

Dorsata takes the security of patient information very seriously and has taken steps to prevent a similar event from occurring in the future, including installing the security patches and updates Metabase has provided to entities who use their software. The notification letters Dorsata sent to potentially affected individuals also include information about steps that individuals can take to protect their information.

Dorsata has established a toll-free call center to answer questions about the incident and related concerns. The toll free phone number is 800-655-5832 and is available from 8:00 am to 8:00 pm ET, Monday through Friday, excluding major holidays.

#5502. Alphabet’s Wing to invest $125M in new delivery drone factory

Wing Aviation LLC today announced plans to spend $125 million on the construction of a new delivery drone factory.

The initiative is part of a broader investment that also encompasses the Alphabet Inc. unit’s research and development teams in California. Additionally, Wing stated that it plans to invest in the communities where it operates. It currently offers deliveries in five U.S. cities and intends to bring its service to 14 more markets soon.

Wing is building its factory in Fort Worth, Texas. The 15,000-square-foot facility is expected to create up to 100 jobs. Wing says it will have capacity to make tens of thousands of delivery drones per year, which should significantly speed up its market expansion efforts.

The Alphabet unit’s drones reportedly have a wingspan of about 4.9 feet. They’re based on a frame made of styrofoam, a foam that mostly consists of trapped air, and carbon fibers. Styrofoam is lightweight and repels water, which comes handy when a drone is navigating challenging weather. The frame’s carbon fibers, in turn, boost its sturdiness.

The drone frame is equipped with 16 electric rotors that enable it to reach speeds of up to 60 miles per hour. Workers at stores that use Wing’s delivery service attach merchandise to its drones via a tether. After a drone takes off, it reels in the tether until the package comes into physical contact with its frame. When it reaches the customer’s house, the drone descends to an altitude of 20 feet and lowers the parcel.

Wing has built a software stack that automates much of the work involved in coordinating deliveries. It picks the most suitable drone for a given delivery run, plans its flight path and ensures that it won’t interfere with other drones. Human safety teams monitor for weather and air traffic changes that may make it necessary to adjust flight plans.

The unit plans to make its delivery service available to more than 40 million Americans by 2027. It’s pursuing the growth initiative in partnership with retailers such as Walmart Inc., which uses its drones to process e-commerce purchases. Last month, the latter company announced plans to make Wing deliveries available at more than 270 stores.

The Alphabet unit also intends to offer its service in Japan. Last month, it teamed up with Tokyo-based internet provider KDDI Corp. to make drone deliveries available to local consumers in 2027.

Although the drone delivery market is in an early stage, Wing already faces a significant amount of competition. In August, Amazon.com Inc. announced plans to make its Prime Air service available in nearly 500 U.S. markets by year’s end. More recently, drone delivery startup Zipline International Inc. raised $1.5 billion in funding at a $21.5 billion valuation.

#5500. Automax.ai Wins Innovation Challenge at LendingTree's 2026 Lender Summit

Automax.ai is modernizing the appraisal process by improving the experience for homeowners, lenders, and appraisers.

CHARLOTTE, N.C., Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LendingTree, Inc. (NASDAQ: TREE), the nation's leading online financial services marketplace, hosted the annual LendingTree Mortgage Summit this week at the Knight Theatre in Charlotte, N.C. bringing together top lenders, industry experts and fintech innovators to assess market outlook, and the evolving mortgage industry. During the event, Automax.ai was named the winner of the 2026 LendingTree Innovation Challenge for its AI-powered platform designed to modernize the property appraisal process.

Nine fintech companies competed in this year's Innovation Challenge, each delivering a seven-minute pitch to a panel of industry judges and Summit attendees. Participants showcased innovative solutions aimed at improving the mortgage experience, increasing operational efficiencies, and addressing challenges facing lenders and borrowers. Automax.ai, an AI-native property appraisal platform, stood out for its approach to simplifying a traditionally time-consuming part of the mortgage process.

Presented by founder and CEO Humza Ahmed, Automax.ai demonstrated how its technology combines digital property inspections, 3D modeling and artificial intelligence to streamline the appraisal process from start to finish. Rather than relying exclusively on traditional, in-person inspections, the platform enables a certified data collector or homeowner to conduct a guided video walkthrough of a property, capturing more than 800 data points, including details about the condition and quality of flooring, ceilings and other property features.

The information is used to generate a detailed 3D model that appraisers can review and verify. Depending on loan eligibility and applicable requirements, the process may support an appraisal waiver or allow an appraiser to use Automax.ai's suite of AI-powered tools to complete the appraisal report.

The platform also provides lenders, underwriters and processors with greater visibility into the status of an appraisal throughout the process. Automax.ai's end-to-end approach delivers average appraisal turnaround times of one to three days, with reports completed within 24 hours following inspection. The company also reports savings of approximately $50 to $100 compared with traditional appraisals, offering the potential to reduce costs and delays in the homebuying process.

Innovation challenge participants were evaluated by judges and audience members across six criteria: increased conversion and originations, ability to implement, market relevance, product quality & UI/UX, and demo quality and salesmanship. The judges panel included Jessica Gardner, CMO of Armed Forces Bank and Academy Bank; Erin Dee, SVP, Chief Innovation Officer at BankSouth Mortgage; and Chad Smith, CEO of Envoy Mortgage.

"This year's Innovation Challenge demonstrated the creativity and entrepreneurial spirit driving the mortgage industry forward," said Will Adams, Head of Sales at LendingTree. "All nine participating companies presented compelling solutions to some of the challenges lenders face today. Automax.ai stood out for its practical approach to addressing a critical part of the mortgage process, with technology that has the potential to reduce costs, accelerate timelines, and improve the experience for lenders, borrowers and appraisers."

Through initiatives like the Innovation Challenge, LendingTree is connecting industry leaders with emerging innovators, spotlighting solutions that help lenders operate more efficiently while creating a simpler, more transparent experience for consumers. Automax.ai's recognition reflects the growing opportunity for AI-powered technology to address longstanding industry challenges and deliver meaningful improvements throughout the mortgage journey.

LendingTree is one of the nation's largest, most experienced online financial platforms, created to give consumers the power to win financially.  LendingTree provides customers with access to the best offers on loans, credit cards, insurance and more through its network of approximately 770 financial partners.  Since its founding, LendingTree has helped millions of customers obtain financing, save money, and improve their financial and credit health in their personal journeys. With a portfolio of innovative products and tools and personalized financial recommendations, LendingTree helps customers achieve everyday financial wins.

LendingTree, Inc. is headquartered in Charlotte, NC. For more information, please visit www.lendingtree.com.
