#5451. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5450. Would You Take the Money? Microsoft Is Offering Employees Its Biggest Buyout Offer to Date.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The tech giant offered buyouts to a quarter of its workforce as it looks to reduce spending.

Two weeks ago, Microsoft presented 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its workforce, with an enticing offer. They could choose to leave Microsoft of their own accord in exchange for a severance package.

“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,” chief people officer Amy Coleman said in a memo to workers in late October.

According to a new report from The New York Times, Microsoft employees flocked to an internal website within an hour of the buyout announcement to find out if they had received an offer.

So many workers were checking at once that employees speculated that traffic had overwhelmed the site.

A handful of Microsoft employees who spoke with the Times said that the buyout offer added strain to an already tense relationship between employees and leadership. They said the buyout proposal arrived amid rising pressure to adopt AI, frustration over flat pay and deepening worries about job security.

The voluntary exit offer is the biggest in the company’s history and marks Microsoft’s second buyout this year.

For Microsoft employees, a buyout means weighing the options. Is the payment enough to make leaving worthwhile?

Workers look at the financial incentive offered by the buyout and weigh it against household expenses, health insurance costs and time needed to find another job. They usually take stock of their savings and consider if they are at risk of layoffs later.

If not enough people choose to accept the offer, Microsoft could resort to layoffs to cut costs. Buyouts are often “a precursor to layoffs,” Lindsay Witcher, a senior executive at career transition firm Randstad RiseSmart, said in an interview with CNBC in 2023.

A Microsoft spokesperson told Bloomberg that workers who accept this buyout offer will receive benefits similar to a regular severance package.

When Microsoft cut U.S. jobs earlier this year, its severance terms guaranteed at least 60 days of base pay. For most employees, the package topped out at 39 weeks of base pay, with the amount determined by their level and length of service, per Business Insider.

The spokesperson added that the buyout applies to employees on select teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K and India. Some employees on teams working on data centers, sales and marketing do not qualify for the buyout.

Eligible employees have until the first week of December to decide if they want to accept the buyout, according to GeekWire. Their departures are scheduled for the end of the year, per CNBC.

Microsoft told GeekWire that the buyout is not a sign that it needs fewer workers. Instead, the tech giant said the measure was one way it was adjusting to shifting business priorities.

Microsoft’s workforce numbered 223,000 people at the end of June, according to its annual filings. That headcount has been relatively flat since 2022, when the company started pouring more money into AI and data centers.

#5449. Anthropic debuts Claude Fable, Mythos 5.2 models, priced 20% below OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra

Anthropic debuted Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on Monday, the company’s answer to OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, which came out in early September.

The new models, which could be Anthropic’s last big releases before its IPO, claim to offer higher performance than Astra at a lower price point—a key factor for earning and retaining customers in a world where professionals seem quick to switch to models based on cost, as long as the performance holds up.

The launch is critical for Anthropic as it seeks to re-accelerate revenue growth, following a third quarter slowdown revealed in latest S-1 filing with the SEC.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are 20% cheaper than Astra for ordinary input and output tasks, at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, compared to $10 and $50, respectively, for GPT-6 Astra. Tokens are the unit of information AI model process. One token of English language text is equivalent to about a word-and-a-half. For prompts with large amounts of information, such as documents, the cost advantage is more pronounced. Anthropic’s new models are 80% cheaper, at 20 cents per million cached tokens compared to one dollar per million cached tokens for GPT-6 Astra.

Anthropic reports impressive results from its pre-release testing. The new models “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications,” the company said.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 perform better than its competitors on coding evaluation benchmarks, Anthropic said, noting that over 90% of the company’s own code is written by AI. While Anthropic’s Claude Code product gained an early lead among programmers, OpenAI’s Codex has gained ground in recent months due to its lower pricing, The Information reported in late October. The combination of lower pricing plus superior performance, if the company’s claims hold up in real-world testing, could help win them back.

The new models are best when used for the “most ambitious, open-ended technical work,” Anthropic said. In other words, they’re competing with Astra at the frontier. However, for daily tasks, Anthropic recommends its customers use its more cost-effective model, Opus 5.5. That model is more expensive than its direct competitor from OpenAI, GPT-6.1 Sol, although it still could end up being a better deal if it yields a high quality result more often. That’s for users to decide as they inevitably begin to try Anthropic’s latest releases and weigh options on a daily basis.

Anthropic is also trying to compete with OpenAI on cybersecurity tasks, such as finding and fixing vulnerabilities in code. The company claims an unnamed security company “found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested.” Late last week, OpenAI debuted a cybersecurity-focused model, GPT-6 Cyber.

The new Anthropic models also reportedly solved two theoretical physics problems related to black holes, and identified a way to speed up research into gene therapies. In light of OpenAI making headlines for solving mathematics proofs that have eluded academics for decades—most notably the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem—Anthropic is highlighting its new models’ mathematics chops as well.

A team of 1,000 agents powerd by Fable 5.2 produced a formalization, or translation of a mathematical proof into a format a computer can check step by step, in 30 hours, compared with 11 days for a previous, unreleased research version of Claude. In a subtle jab at the mathematics community’s backlash to OpenAI pouring millions of dollars into solving proofs and upending the field, Anthropic notes that its quick formalizations can help human mathematicians check their proofs faster so they can “spend more time exploring novel ideas.”

One unique area Anthropic seems to be leaning into more than OpenAI is hardware and robotics. The new models were allegedly able to design and produce three working electronic devices, complete with circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software, based on a one-paragraph prompt.

Finally, Anthropic highlighted the models’ safety features, including safeguards that block “high-risk cyber activities including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology.”

Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Mythos 5.2 access is application-only for cybersecurity professionals and life sciences researchers. Claude Enterprise customers can also access Mythos 5.2 through Anthropic’s Claude Security product.

#5448. Customers Suing McDonald’s In Chicago Are Not Lovin’ the McRib

A federal judge says customers could reasonably expect a sandwich called the McRib to contain actual ribs.

The McRib may truly only be back for a limited time.

On Oct. 30, U.S. District Judge April M. Perry in Chicago ruled that a proposed class-action McRib lawsuit against McDonald’s can move forward. Filed by four consumers last December, the suit says the highly popular sandwich contains no rib meat. The plaintiffs allege the patty is made from cheaper pork parts like shoulder, heart and tripe and pressed into the shape of a rack of ribs.

The company describes the meat as “seasoned boneless pork,” according to The New York Times, and lists its ingredients on its website. It argued that the “Mc” prefix only marks the sandwich as a McDonald’s product and doesn’t promise rib meat. McDonald’s also denies using organ meat.

But Perry didn’t buy it. Sure, a McFlurry may not contain a literal flurry, but she found it reasonable for a customer to expect rib meat in something called the McRib. “The court is not persuaded by defendant’s many arguments that it would be unreasonable or fanciful to think the McRib contains rib meat,” she wrote. The suit seeks unspecified damages and an end to the McRib’s current marketing. Perry dismissed five claims but let the deception, fraud and unjust enrichment claims proceed.

#5447. Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 1:39 pm

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

#5446. Vietnam’s cheap coffee may lose its edge as the EU tightens sustainability rules, Nestlé Vietnam’s chair warns

Vietnam’s cheap coffee is “no longer going to be attractive to export” as the European Union tightens its sustainability rules, Binu Jacob, chairman and managing director of Nestlé Vietnam, warned last week at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit in Ho Chi Minh City on Nov. 3.

The Southeast Asian nation is the world’s second-largest coffee producer and the largest producer of robusta, the variety largely used in instant coffee. Europe is the world’s largest coffee market, accounting for about 24% of global consumption, according to the European Coffee Federation. That gives the bloc’s standards outsized importance for producers.

“Vietnam was always known to produce cheap coffee, but cheap coffee is no longer going to be attractive to export because [the] EU is coming up with very stringent norms,” Jacob said. “So if we don’t go up the value chain and create coffee that is sustainable and that meets the very high standards, we will be unable to export.”

The EU Deforestation Regulation applies to most companies from Dec. 30, 2026, though some smaller businesses will not need to comply until later in 2027. The regulation aims to curb deforestation and forest degradation linked to the production of certain commodities, and to reduce the bloc’s contribution to greenhouse gas emissions and biodiversity loss.

Hanoi is working with Brussels on compliance. The multiyear, EU-backed SustainCoffee project aims to help the country’s coffee sector meet international environmental, social, and governance standards, and support more than 400 coffee-related businesses while indirectly benefit an estimated 1.4 million farmers and workers in the supply chain.

Nestlé has applied its global research and development capabilities, partnering with the Western Highlands Agriculture and Forestry Science Institute, a prominent agricultural research institution, to develop a coffee plantlet “best suited for the soil conditions in the Central Highlands,” Jacob said.

The company propagates the plantlets through tissue culture. “From one leaf of this coffee plant, you can actually make 2,000 trees, and this is what we’ve been doing in the last 15 years,” he explained.

“We have made 100 million plantlets of this disease-resistant coffee plantlet, and then distributed it at subsidized rates to farmers all over central Vietnam,” he said. “As a result, the productivity and the yield of coffee today in Vietnam is three times that of the global average, and this can be replicated anywhere in the world.”

Still, Jacob cast the rules as a chance for Vietnam to move up the value chain. “With small farms, it’s quite easy to move from the old ways of traditional farming to regenerative farming,” he said. “Once you do that, Vietnam has a competitive advantage to export more and ensure that more value stays here.”

#5445. Your Next Customer Is an AI Agent. Here’s How to Market to It.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AEO and GEO are chapter one, but the next big shift is evolving further down the purchase funnel

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When most people hear “AI marketing,” they think of using AI to do marketing. This may mean writing copy faster, generating ad creative, automating outbound sequences, etc. That’s useful and has a huge impact on how marketers approach their jobs, but it’s not what I’m talking about.

I’m talking about marketing to AI. Specifically, to the agents that are starting to shop on behalf of people.

The first wave of AI search optimization (AEO, GEO, AIO, pick your acronym) was built around one shape of AI: the chatbot or answer engine. A shopper asks a question, an LLM writes an answer, and somewhere in that answer your brand shows up, or it doesn’t.

That framing got a lot right, but it is still largely rooted in how we think about traditional search, the only real difference being the shift from keywords to questions. That said, it has sparked a new discipline within marketing, one where many brands are tracking and investing energy in understanding how AI models read their site and content, which sources AI cites when answering brand-relevant questions, and how they stack up against competitors across LLM responses.

All of this is important, but just the tip of the iceberg. What marketers need to do next is evolve their GEO strategies to not only ensure their brand appears in the first answer, but also to ensure that as a shopper travels through the full buyer’s journey within the same AI search conversation, their products and services remain relevant and ultimately win the customer decision. The later portion of the journey used to happen after a shopper clicked from their initial Google search to your website. Now it lives entirely between the shopper and their agent.

This is where we’ve seen brands quietly lose. When my team ran 320 simulated shopper conversations, nearly three in ten brand mentions never turned into a recommendation. The brand showed up in the answer, and then somewhere further down the conversation the agent picked someone else. That lines up with independent research showing AI shopping assistants get worse as conversations get longer. Getting mentioned and getting picked are two different things, and right now most brands are only measuring the first one.

It is important to note that not all agents look like chatbots, and as AI Search evolves into new formats, so must our marketing strategies.

Look at Meta’s Muse. It launched on Sept. 8 and quickly climbed to the top of the App Store. It’s not really a chatbot; it’s a personal agent that runs on its own cloud machine, opens its own browser, scans retail sites, compares prices, and checks out for you. It keeps a shopping profile on each person, tracking their actions and tastes.

And Muse is one example, but there are agents that live in text messages, inside browsers, in glasses, and in voice. Many brands and retailers are building their own agentic shopping experience too. Each iteration and version finds products differently, reads them differently, and ultimately guides their users down buyer journeys in different ways. These are all new potential blind spots that we, as marketers, must learn to address and influence to reach our shoppers via their agent.

They pull from everywhere. In one early test, most of Muse’s product picks came from live websites rather than Meta’s own catalog, even though the catalog offered far more options. Your site, your feeds and every catalog you’re listed in all count.

They act, not just answer. An agent that can check out has to get through your site first. Amazon has already blocked Muse. Plenty of brands are blocking agents without knowing it, through bot protection built for a world where bots were the threat.

They remember. A profile that says “Wide feet, and need extra support for bad knees” shapes every future recommendation. That’s potential brand loyalty, written down by a machine.

They report to a human. Muse asks for approval before it makes a purchase. The agent has to justify its pick and give its reasons.

That last point matters more than most brands realize, and it’s a big part of where that three-in-ten number comes from. Agents don’t just find you, they do a lot of the “choosing” on behalf of their shopper. In our simulations, in which shoppers were looking for headphones under $150, the shift from mentioning a brand to recommending it occurred once the shopper provided a budget. One premium brand was mentioned in 82 answers and recommended in none. Another got named as a premium option and then dropped as soon as the price cap came up, losing the chance to sell premium value to justify a higher cost.

Meanwhile, a value brand went from never being recommended when budget came up to almost always being recommended afterward, which is a price-fit story, not a trust story. The brands that dropped off weren’t unknown to the agent, they just didn’t fit the shopper’s constraints, which meant the agent had nothing to justify the pick with when it came time to choose.

Here’s the issue with AEO and GEO as labels: they name the interface.

A lot of people, Forrester included, are now saying the agent is your new customer. I don’t think that’s quite right. The customer hasn’t changed; the person is still the one you’re trying to win, but more and more they’re represented by an agent that does the buying for them, on a journey we aren’t used to. That agent is both a new gatekeeper and a new audience, and marketers need strategies for both.

So I think the more useful frame is marketing to agents. Not instead of GEO, but as an extension of. If GEO is how you show up when an agent answers, then marketing to agents more broadly is how you win. Being able to influence the entire AI assistant shopping journey is the target we need to keep in view. I think about this as “AI Search marketing” broadly.

We’ve seen this before. “Internet marketing” eventually split into search, social, email, ecommerce, affiliate and a dozen other disciplines. Marketing to agents will split the same way. The brands that do well will be the ones that start treating the agent as a buyer worth winning now, not a bot to block, while the shapes are still settling.

You don’t need to rebuild anything this quarter. A few moves go a long way:

People still want the right product, at a fair price, from a brand they trust. What’s new is that more of the legwork goes to software that reads everything, never sees your homepage hero, and remembers how it went.

Market to the buyer, win the customer. Build for the whole job, not the initial chat response.

When most people hear “AI marketing,” they think of using AI to do marketing. This may mean writing copy faster, generating ad creative, automating outbound sequences, etc. That’s useful and has a huge impact on how marketers approach their jobs, but it’s not what I’m talking about.

I’m talking about marketing to AI. Specifically, to the agents that are starting to shop on behalf of people.

The first wave of AI search optimization (AEO, GEO, AIO, pick your acronym) was built around one shape of AI: the chatbot or answer engine. A shopper asks a question, an LLM writes an answer, and somewhere in that answer your brand shows up, or it doesn’t.

#5444. Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:01 amNovember 5, 2026 at 7:01 am

Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.

Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.

A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.

Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.”

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC, which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”

Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.

“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

#5443. AI Is Changing the Economics of SaaS Partnerships. Here’s How Founders Can Capitalize.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is reshaping the SaaS partner model, creating opportunities beyond traditional referral commissions and low-margin services.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A typical SaaS referral deal gives a partner 10-15% of first-year revenue, rarely enough to support sales, implementation and future growth. As SaaS made software easier to buy and deploy, much of the surrounding work became repeatable, pushing partners toward lower-margin services. Without a more profitable business to build around the platform, they will invest elsewhere.

AI gives partners something SaaS gradually took away: high-value work built on the platform, shaped by the customer’s context and sold as expertise rather than access. Not every AI engagement will be unique, nor should it be. The reusable parts like connectors, retrieval patterns, evaluation frameworks and managed operations will become more standard. But the decisions that make an AI system useful do not travel so easily from one customer to another. Which workflow should change? Which data can be used? Where does human review belong? What counts as a good answer, and who is accountable when it is wrong?

The building blocks may be familiar, but making the workflow safe, useful and adopted is not. It relies on industry judgment that the partner has built from years of being the person the client calls when something breaks.

This is not an argument that every partner should go train a model, or that every SaaS company should suddenly become a services business. Most customer deployments will be about workflow design, permitted data, integration, evaluation, governance and adoption, not fine-tuning a foundation model. The point is simpler: AI creates a new layer of work above the subscription, and the partners best placed to capture it are the ones who know the customer’s business well enough to make that layer valuable.

Futurum Research’s 2H 2026 partner survey found that 71% of active partners named custom application development as a primary growth driver, even as sentiment toward packaged enterprise software weakened. But that does not mean every bespoke build will be profitable. It does suggest that customers are looking beyond generic software for tailored engineering and that partners see more room in services than in a shrinking resale margin.

For SaaS founders, that changes the question from “How do we get partners to refer more deals?” to “What can partners build profitably with us?” Start by running the full math: referral and renewal income, plus the gross profit from partner-delivered implementation and AI services, minus the cost of acquiring and serving the account. If a partner can create a healthy contribution margin while making the product more useful to the customer, the program has a foundation. If it cannot, a higher referral percentage is just a more expensive version of the same problem.

The program should then make that work easier to do well. Give capable partners a sandbox that resembles production, not just a demo login. Train them on integration, evaluation, governance and escalation — not only on product features. Certify them against real use cases. Bring the strongest partners into the harder solutions early, before the vendor has decided every implementation detail in-house. That is how a platform becomes a place where partners can build expertise instead of merely resell a discount.

Measure the result accordingly. Referred ARR still matters, but it is only part of the picture. Track services revenue and margin where they can be observed, time to production, active use, product adoption, support burden, retention and the customer outcome the solution was designed to improve. Outcome-based incentives can work, too, if they are tied to milestones the partner can actually influence: a verified deployment, adoption by an agreed user group, a successful evaluation or a retained account after a defined period.

None of this removes the need for discipline. A vendor still needs clear data rights, guardrails, support boundaries and a view of who is accountable when a workflow fails. Partners need room to earn services revenue without creating a maintenance burden the vendor cannot support. Those are not reasons to stay with the old model. They are the operating details that turn the AI thesis into a business model.

The point is not that AI work will never commoditize. Some of it will, and it should. The point is that AI gives partners a larger, more defensible role while the work still depends on customer data, workflow knowledge and practical judgment. A program built around that role is harder to reduce to a commission table. It gives partners more reason to invest, gives customers more value from the platform, and gives the vendor something more durable than a better percentage to compete on.

A typical SaaS referral deal gives a partner 10-15% of first-year revenue, rarely enough to support sales, implementation and future growth. As SaaS made software easier to buy and deploy, much of the surrounding work became repeatable, pushing partners toward lower-margin services. Without a more profitable business to build around the platform, they will invest elsewhere.

AI gives partners something SaaS gradually took away: high-value work built on the platform, shaped by the customer’s context and sold as expertise rather than access. Not every AI engagement will be unique, nor should it be. The reusable parts like connectors, retrieval patterns, evaluation frameworks and managed operations will become more standard. But the decisions that make an AI system useful do not travel so easily from one customer to another. Which workflow should change? Which data can be used? Where does human review belong? What counts as a good answer, and who is accountable when it is wrong?

#5442. Nvidia built itself around one man. A scandal is testing that bet

Few executives loom larger over a single company than Jensen Huang does at Nvidia. His 33-year reign as CEO, and the success he’s overseen during the AI boom, have made him a hugely powerful force at the $4.3 trillion company. Now, the linchpin of the AI industry will test the limits of its corporate governance and succession planning.

After Huang on Sunday acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, Nvidia’s board announced an investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The admission followed reporting about his relationship with a woman whom U.S. authorities concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times. The board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that its inquiry would examine “all available information.”

The trick for investigators, according to business and law experts, is that they are investigating, and will potentially consider ousting, perhaps the most critical executive to America’s AI success. And they will do so under a company power structure in which Huang reigns as an outsized decision-maker.

Huang is “synonymous with Nvidia, and Nvidia is synonymous with him, and he and Nvidia are synonymous with AI, so he’s bound up in the company’s identity much more than other cases,” Brian Burke, founder of Burke Law & Strategy and a corporate board advisor, told Fortune. Nvidia is “a paradigm out there that people look up to and they say, ‘Oh, I want to be like Nvidia.’ Other CEOs say, ‘I want to be like Jensen Huang.’ So, it’s really almost like a cult.”

Huang, 63, has set up a unique structure around him at Nvidia that has concentrated decision-making in his hands. He has been CEO for 33 years, astonishingly long for any company. Nvidia has no chief operating officer, and Huang has about 60 direct reports, creating uncertainty about who is next in line to lead.

Huang is known to play a central role in strategic and technical decisions, and the success he’s had since the AI boom got underway in late 2022 has only strengthened his grip on the company and the AI industry at large. He has become something of a celebrity in the tech world, with followers wearing leather jackets to copy him and fans pursuing him at corporate events for a selfie or a signature. He has also gotten close to the Trump administration, which has counted on him for counsel on AI and taken him on foreign trips.

Huang is Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, with a 3.56% stake, but he doesn’t have any super-voting shares like Mark Zuckerberg has at Meta Platforms. He leads what is the world’s second most valuable company. (Its shares sank more than 4% on Monday after he admitted to the affaire.) Nvidia has been estimated to control about 90% of the market for high-powered GPU computer chips used in AI data centers.

The company has also operated without a chief compliance officer. In a September 2022 staff at the Securities and Exchange Commission asked for more detail about board risk oversight, whether the company had such an officer and to whom that person reported, and about its overall structure. Nvidia has said it has a compliance committee made up of its chief financial officer, executive vice president of operations, and senior vice president of human resources, which it says “ensures communication of and adherence to all NVIDIA policies.”

There are few other cases, if any, that resemble Nvidia’s current situation. Corporate executives whose romantic liaisons have derailed their careers are common enough. In 2019, McDonald’s fired CEO Steve Easterbrook over a consensual relationship with an employee that violated company policy. The bigger scandal came afterward: the company discovered additional undisclosed relationships, sued to recover his exit compensation, and ultimately recovered cash and equity valued at $105 million. In this case however, the romantic liaison involves an alleged spy and the CEO of the dominant company building some of the U.S.’s most valuable technology.

Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University who has studied CEO succession practices, told Fortune that Nvidia’s concentration of so much power and decision-making in Huang now makes it very vulnerable to what comes next.

“The board has made a mistake by not having a clearly outlined succession plan that’s been telegraphed to the market for a year or two,” Schloetzer said. “They find themselves at the day of reckoning, and it’s a sudden and perhaps forced one, rather than a relay situation where they have time to figure it out as they go.”

Hui Chen, a former federal prosecutor who served as the U.S. Justice Department’s first compliance counsel expert from 2015 to 2017, told Fortune that corporate risk efforts tend to focus on leaks from rank and file staff members, and companies don’t pay as much attention to similar risks by high-level executives.

Schloetzer and other experts said it’s plausible for the board to appoint an interim CEO or have Nvidia’s lead independent director—Stephen Neal, chairman emeritus and senior counsel at law firm Cooley LLP—as interim CEO if Huang steps down. Another option for an interim could be Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress. The concern with any next-CEO plan is how the market will receive the decision, since Huang is seen as critical to Nvidia’s success.

Huang also has children who work at Nvidia and could be options to succeed him. Spencer Huang is a director of product management, and his daughter, Madison, is a senior director of product marketing. Both have reportedly worked on robotics at the company. His son-in-law, Nico Caprez, is vice president of global AI infrastructure growth.

The board could oust Huang at the end of its investigation, or Huang could have to step down before then, Burke said. He could also leave the CEO role but stay on in another capacity.

In media interviews over the years, Huang has dismissed conventional succession planning, saying his approach is to continually transfer his knowledge to colleagues. He has also said he hopes Nvidia’s next CEO already works at the company, even though Nvidia has not publicly identified a successor.

#5441. Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:54 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:03 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time.

Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics.

“You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.”

After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells.

Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB), her immune-system research well in the past.

Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues.

Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved.

“Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.”

Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad.

“She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.”

When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments.

“It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April.

One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene.

The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow.

“It was a really exciting time,” Brunkow said. “It took a lot of problem solving and troubleshooting to get to the answer.”

The scientists narrowed their search to 20 genes on the X chromosome and began painstakingly sequencing them. In the final gene, they found a tiny error — two extra DNA letters inserted into the sequence that rendered the protein useless.

Working with Ramsdell and other collaborators, the researchers identified the mouse gene and showed that mutations in its human counterpart, FOXP3, cause a rare autoimmune disorder called IPEX.

“It was nice to pull the story together. So we published a couple of nice papers. We filed patent inventions. We went to conferences and talked about it,” Brunkow said. “And then in 2004, the company closed down.”

Brunkow stayed friends with Ramsdell and followed developments in the field, but her own interests took her elsewhere. She was drawn less to one particular disease than to the challenge of finding a tiny genetic change that could have an enormous biological effect — and potentially point toward a treatment.

Meanwhile, other researchers were building on the discoveries.

Later research established the gene’s essential role in regulatory T cells, or Tregs — cells that restrain immune responses and protect the body from attacking itself.

“I didn’t actually understand the extent to which our publications kind of blew open a whole new area in immunology,” Brunkow said.

That work is now reaching patients. In June, the FDA approved Tregzi, a treatment incorporating regulatory T cells that helps prevent a serious complication of donor stem cell transplants in adults with blood cancers.

At ISB, Brunkow has embraced a broader view of biology. The organization takes a holistic approach to medical research, bringing together scientists in areas including cancer, infectious diseases and chronic illnesses.

For her, it is a natural progression from studying individual genes to investigating the complex networks in which they operate. The ultimate goal is personalized medicine: understanding what pushes someone from health toward disease, detecting those changes early and finding ways to intervene.

The Nobel recognition has given Brunkow a chance to broaden her impact beyond research — a platform to advocate for issues she cares about. That includes sustained research funding, support for women and other underrepresented groups in science, and stronger STEM education. She also wants to encourage scientists to support one another and work well together — the qualities she encountered in that UW fruit fly lab.

“You’ve got to figure out how to play well with others,” Brunkow said. “It makes science more fun. It makes science move faster.”

#5440. You Don’t Need a Full-Time Executive to Get C-Suite Expertise. Here’s Why.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

For entrepreneurs, there are lots of good reasons to hire on a fractional basis — but it might not be right for everyone. Here’s my take.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Hiring full-time workers is a commitment, especially at the C-suite level. As a solopreneur myself, it took me a long time before I had the resources to bring anyone on to help shoulder the responsibilities of running my business.

But a lot has changed since I launched my company back in 2006. Now, fractional executives—leaders who share their expertise with organizations on a part-time basis—are quickly becoming the norm. In fact, research has found that the number of workers describing themselves as “fractional” has tripled since 2018; among executives, the most common limited roles are CFOs, followed by CMOs.

For entrepreneurs, there are lots of good reasons to hire on a fractional basis. The right fractional executive can bring valuable expertise, fresh perspective and strategic guidance without requiring the long-term investment of a full-time hire. But it might not be right for everyone. Here’s my take.

Several factors have conspired to create the recent boom in fractional work. Post-Covid-19, more people are seeking out flexible roles and the ability to work multiple part-time jobs. At the same time, a tough job market has produced a surplus of highly skilled workers, while many companies don’t have the funds to fill those roles full-time.

Leadership roles are also simply growing more complex. Between the proliferation of hybrid work and AI adoption, it stands to reason that expertise is also becoming more varied. In general, high level roles are changing, with AI automating several functions previously handled by executives, like operations and reporting. On the other hand, demand for a la carte, specialized skills are on the rise — maybe your organization needs someone fluent in transitioning to an AI-powered workforce, but only on a limited-time basis.

You’d be forgiven for thinking fractional executives are just consultants by another, buzzier name. But the truth is they’re quite different.

The main distinction is that, while they do work on a part-time basis, fractional executives are embedded in your team. They make decisions that drive outcomes and are responsible for what happens as a result.

Consultants, on the other hand, operate outside the organization. They make recommendations, but are not ultimately accountable for how things turn out. For example, a consultant can analyze your pricing strategy and show you a presentation on how they think it can be improved. A fractional CFO, on the other hand, will rebuild the pricing model themselves, and answer for the numbers at the quarter’s end.

Before you hire someone touting themselves as a fractional executive, dig into the details of what they’re offering and make sure they — and you — understand the difference.

Fractional work may be a product of our current moment, but it’s also unlikely to go away any time soon.

For entrepreneurs, the perks of such roles are many. Benefits packages, equity and long-term salary commitments are not part of the equation. You get the expertise without the long-term overhead, and you can scale the relationship up or down as your needs change.

But fractional isn’t free of tradeoffs, and it isn’t right for every role. Start by asking a few questions:

It’s entirely possible that a fractional hire can turn into a full-time offer once the time is right. But understanding the role, its limitations and whether it’s the appropriate fit for your business is key. A fractional hire doesn’t need to feel like a compromise, because it shouldn’t be. Handled correctly, it’s a deliberate way to get the right expertise at the right time, without pretending your company needs something it doesn’t.

Hiring full-time workers is a commitment, especially at the C-suite level. As a solopreneur myself, it took me a long time before I had the resources to bring anyone on to help shoulder the responsibilities of running my business.

#5439. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5438. California Wine Country Saw Its Earliest Harvest in Decades. Here’s How a 67-Year-Old Business Navigated It — And What Every Entrepreneur Can Learn.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From supply chain to sustainability, Rodney Strong Vineyards knows what it takes to succeed.

Napa Valley and Sonoma, two of California’s top-growing wine regions, recently underwent their earliest grape harvest in decades. In response to a record-breaking March heat wave and early bud break, grape-picking started in July. The process typically starts in early to mid-August.

Fortunately, wine-growers and -makers across the region turn to harvest playbooks that have withstood the test of time.

One of them is 67-year-old Rodney Strong Vineyards in Healdsburg, California.

Rodney Strong, who had a brief stint in the Navy before dancing on Broadway in New York City, retired from performing life and established his namesake winery in 1959. He brought on Rick Sayre as winemaker in 1979.

In 1989, the Klein family purchased Rodney Strong Vineyards. A graduate of Stanford’s MBA program, Tom Klein met Strong and Sayre a decade prior when his team at McKinsey & Company was hired to evaluate the winery.

To this day, more than six decades on, a successful harvest at Rodney Strong Vineyards strikes the balance between art and science. (Just one example of many: The preferred light pink shade of Rodney Strong’s rosé requires bringing those grapes in under the cover of night, before any heat can degrade them).

During the final days of 2026’s harvest, Entrepreneur visited Rodney Strong Vineyards and its estate vineyard Rockaway Vineyards to learn more about the business’s approach.

The takeaways from chief winemaking and operations officer Justin Seidenfeld and head of winegrowing Allison Dericco can ripen any business for success, whether or not they’re focused on the vine.

Businesses should never underestimate the value of knowing their supply chain — and its nuances — to ensure their product delivers on quality every time.

On the topic of Rodney Strong’s very intentional rosé: Heat is the most immediate logistical risk to grape quality between a morning harvest at Rockaway Vineyards and the crush pad.

“As the fruit sits in the sun, it will begin to dessicate,” Seidenfeld says. “That will change the balance of the fruit.”

That’s why the team starts picking grapes at dawn and fast tracks them to the winery. The fruit is kept in an air-conditioned space until it’s sorted and put into a tank for fermentation, Seidenfeld notes.

These days, businesses across industries can drill down on their supply chain with advanced technologies that gather data at every touchpoint, putting an innovative twist on operational fundamentals that comes with a major competitive advantage.

In a similar vein, businesses have to understand their assets and how to prioritize them for long-term success.

Rodney Strong boasts a robust wine portfolio. A premium, small-lot Rockaway grape experiences a different crush and fermentation than a larger-lot grape destined for the broader Sonoma County or Estate tiers.

Rodney Strong’s Sonoma and Estate wines are larger, so they require a less precise “sweet spotting” technique compared to Rockaway and other reserve wines, Seidenfeld says.

Still, those grapes destined for the broader tier are managed closely to ensure quality.

“[We rely on] careful site development to keep the block as uniform as possible and the implantation of deficit irrigation to help find as much balance across the whole block as possible,” Seidenfeld says.

What’s more, any business can put this into practice by zeroing in on an often overlooked strategy: dynamic resource allocation, which shifts money, talent and management attention to areas where they can generate the most value.

Data analysis plays an important role in business operations and risk mitigation, but well-informed intuition can be just as valuable.

At the vineyard, whether a block of grapes hangs on the vine for one more day or gets picked as soon as possible comes down to chemistry and gut feeling.

Seidenfeld says the decision on when to harvest is the most important one the winery makes every year.

“While we use the data from the samples we pull to guide us, the final call on when to harvest is made through our eyes and ears and taste and not with what we get from the lab,” Seidenfeld explains.

Some degree of risk is inevitable in business, but entrepreneurs who pay attention to the pressures related to growth, culture and information management can sharpen their decision-making ability when it counts — and minimize potential losses.

Businesses that embrace sustainability not only foster positive consumer sentiment, but also protect their long-term product viability and bottom line.

Rodney Strong became the first carbon neutral winery in Sonoma County in 2009. The team works to create a balanced growing environment with practices like water conservation, soil management and biodiversity encouragement, maintaining healthy vines and managing stress as they develop, Dericco notes.

Additionally, using tools like soil moisture monitoring, weather stations and plant-based measurements allows the team to make more precise farming decisions, particularly when it comes to irrigation.

“While our carbon neutrality and waste reduction efforts have broader environmental benefits, it’s these everyday practices in the vineyard that directly influence vine health, fruit development, and ultimately, wine quality,” Dericco says.

The lesson for business owners? Consider sustainability a building block, not an afterthought, to ensure genuine messaging and meaningful collaboration.

#5437. Franklin Templeton Will Use OpenAI ChatGPT to Predict Crypto

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

In early November 2026, OpenAI published a detailed customer story highlighting how Franklin Templeton, the global asset manager overseeing roughly $1.8 trillion in assets, is integrating advanced AI tools into its investment research process.

The firm is not simply experimenting with chatbots for note-taking. It is systematically building AI-powered workflows to help portfolio managers compare competing research views, surface overlooked risks, and make better-informed investment decisions.

#5436. No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:45 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:45 am

If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal.

Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat, which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode.

Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized.

“I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.”

“It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head.

Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through.

The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders.

“Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards.

Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners.

Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him.

Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights.

Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out.

O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said.

When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said.

Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal.

“We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said.

Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024. Huffman also runs GrowthHit, a Seattle-based growth marketing agency he founded in 2016.

Huffman came across Neat through a GrowthHit client, a sports performance brand whose team had developed the technology. Having grown up in Oklahoma and lived in Texas and New York, Huffman said he knew the pain of hot days when you can “never wear heather gray.” When the client sent him a shirt, his reaction was, “Oh my gosh, this is amazing!”

GrowthHit had been looking for a brand of its own after earlier attempts to launch products didn’t pan out, Huffman said. The agency took over Neat, with the original team continuing to handle product development while GrowthHit ran branding and marketing.

Neat’s net sales grew more than 300% in 2025, to about $700,000, and the company is on track for $1.5 million to $2 million in sales this year, Huffman said.

Huffman credits the growth to basic growth-marketing moves. Neat positioned itself as something other than a regular cotton tee, pushed bundles over single shirts, upgraded its product photos and raised prices.

Neat’s newest shirt, the Sweat Defender Crew, sells for $59.99, with discounts for bundles. Huffman told the Sharks that each shirt costs about $11.70 to make.

The company scaled through Instagram and Facebook ads, going from about $20 a day in ad spend to roughly $2,000 a day.

Its best-known ad pops a water balloon inside a shirt to show the outside staying dry. “We need to be able to demonstrate the product in five seconds, or you’re toast,” Huffman said.

Neat is profitable and hasn’t raised venture funding, Huffman said. He said the company is on track for a 15% profit margin this year.

The company has four employees, two in Seattle and two in Portland. Its shirts are made in Vietnam and sold directly to consumers. They’re not on Amazon or in stores yet, but Huffman said “Shark Tank” could open new sales channels.

Traffic to Neat’s site jumped about 20-fold from the East Coast and Central time zones as soon as the segment aired, Huffman said. The company did more sales during the nine-minute segment than it does on a strong holiday, with a second wave when the show aired on the West Coast.

The most popular color since the show aired is the sage green Huffman and Stelter wore in the tank, which is also the color Neat has the least of in stock.

“Our main priorities right now are making sure the site doesn’t crash and that customer service can keep up,” Huffman said.

#5435. Students Want More Than Degrees. Community Colleges Now Have to Prove Economic Value

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Community colleges are rethinking student success by focusing on living-wage jobs and higher earnings.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Students are increasingly looking beyond earning a college degree or credential. They want to know whether their education will lead to meaningful employment, better earnings, and long-term career opportunities. As expectations shift toward tangible career outcomes, community colleges are facing growing pressure to demonstrate the value of the programs they offer.

A July 2026 report from the Aspen Institute and Columbia University’s Community College Research Center highlights the challenge. According to the research, more than one-third of community college credentials are unlikely to lead directly to living-wage jobs or bachelor’s degrees that provide pathways to such employment. This raises an important question: Are colleges preparing students simply to complete academic programs, or to succeed in the workforce?

Some institutions are already rethinking their approach. Through the Unlocking Opportunity initiative, launched in 2022, 10 community colleges across the United States have been working to align academic programs more closely with employment opportunities and pathways to further education. Between 2022 and 2025, these institutions moved more than 20,000 additional students into programs associated with stronger career and transfer outcomes, representing a 27% increase in enrollment in high-value pathways.

These developments point to a shift in how community colleges are defining student success, placing greater emphasis on the career opportunities and economic mobility that education can create.

As students increasingly prioritize career outcomes, community colleges are reassessing whether their academic programs reflect labor market needs. Rather than relying solely on enrollment demand or existing course offerings, institutions are using employment data, regional workforce trends, and employer partnerships to identify programs that can lead to stronger career opportunities.

This approach is particularly important in sectors facing workforce shortages, where colleges can play a direct role in preparing students for in-demand occupations. By collaborating with employers, institutions can better understand the skills required for specific roles, adapt their curricula, and expand access to practical training opportunities.

At San Antonio College in Texas, this strategy has translated into measurable enrollment growth. To address a regional nursing shortage, the college partnered with healthcare employers to expand clinical training placements, a major constraint on nursing program capacity. According to the Aspen Institute’s July 2026 report, these efforts helped increase enrollment in its selective nursing programs by 71% over three years.

Similarly, Southwest Wisconsin Technical College identified a shortage of radiologic technologists in its region and introduced a radiography program to address the gap. Local hospitals supported the initiative by donating equipment, while the college converted existing space into a training laboratory. The program filled its available places upon launch, demonstrating student demand for training connected to regional employment opportunities.

These examples show how community colleges are taking a more active role in workforce development. Instead of simply offering programs and leaving students to navigate the job market after graduation, institutions are collaborating with employers to create clearer pathways into in-demand occupations. While the long-term employment outcomes of these initiatives are still being evaluated, their early results demonstrate how aligning academic offerings with workforce needs can expand access to career-oriented education.

As the value of higher education comes under greater scrutiny, community colleges are facing a difficult question: Should they continue offering programs that attract students but provide limited opportunities after graduation? Enrollment and completion rates remain important indicators of institutional performance, but they do not necessarily reflect the economic value of a credential.

This is prompting a closer examination of how academic programs align with employment opportunities, graduate earnings, and pathways to further education. Rather than evaluating programs solely on student demand, colleges can use labor market information and graduate outcomes to determine which offerings need to be updated, expanded, or reconsidered.

South Puget Sound Community College in Washington offers a recent example. In 2026, the college’s board voted to close its Paralegal, Culinary Arts, and Baking & Pastry Arts programs following a review of regional employment demand, career outcomes, and financial sustainability. College officials found that many local culinary and baking positions did not require formal qualifications or offer significant wage advantages to credential holders. The decision was also driven by budgetary pressures, with the two food-related programs costing the institution approximately $618,000 annually.

However, measuring program value is not always straightforward. Some credentials prepare students for immediate employment, while others provide foundational education for transfer to four-year institutions. A program with modest short-term earnings may still offer significant long-term value if it helps students pursue advanced qualifications or enter occupations with stronger career progression.

For community colleges, the challenge is not simply to eliminate programs with weaker employment outcomes. It is to ensure that students understand where different educational pathways can lead and that institutions regularly assess whether their offerings deliver on those expectations.

Helping students enter programs with strong career prospects requires more than offering the right courses. Community colleges are increasingly integrating career planning into academic advising to help students understand employment opportunities, potential earnings, and the qualifications needed for their chosen careers.

A 2024 report from the Center for Community College Student Engagement, based on responses from 83,189 students across 199 community colleges, found that more than 90% had chosen a career path, yet many lacked essential information about how to pursue it.

To address this gap, Lane Community College in Oregon uses a Guided Pathways framework to help students explore career options, select programs, and develop academic plans. Technology, including AI-supported advising tools, can further improve access to personalized guidance and help advisors identify students who need additional support.

By connecting academic decisions with career goals earlier, community colleges can help students make more informed choices about their education and future employment.

The path forward requires community colleges to turn these strategies into measurable results. Stronger employer partnerships, regular program evaluations, and proactive career advising must become integral to how institutions operate, rather than isolated initiatives.

The challenge now is to ensure that these changes translate into better employment prospects, higher earnings, and smoother transitions to further education. Ultimately, the institutions that succeed will be those that can demonstrate the economic value of their programs and consistently deliver on the career opportunities they promise students.

They want to know whether their education will lead to meaningful employment, better earnings, and long-term career opportunities. As expectations shift toward tangible career outcomes, community colleges are facing growing pressure to demonstrate the value of the programs they offer.

According to the research, more than one-third of community college credentials are unlikely to lead directly to living-wage jobs or bachelor’s degrees that provide pathways to such employment.
